item.title: Dow futures jump 800 points and Nasdaq soars nearly 3% as stocks rebound from correction with Wall Street still upbeat on 2027
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Clear reporting on market trends and AI impact, with useful vocabulary and context

Investors are poised to begin a short trading week with some early holiday cheer after suffering the worst loss in more than six years.

Futures tied to the Dow Jones industrial average surged 798 points, or 1.66%. S&P 500 futures shot up 2.11%, and Nasdaq futures soared 2.75%.

That came after the Dow and Nasdaq notched their biggest weekly declines since the early days of the COVID-10 pandemic, while the S&P 500 saw its steepest such drop since April 2025, when President Donald Trump stunned markets with his “Liberation Day” tariffs.

The S&P 500 and Dow joined the Nasdaq in correction territory. Tech shares have led the selloff as Wall Street fears the AI boom is about to go bust. The downtrend began after the midterm elections handed victories to Democrats more skeptical of data centers.

But the Nvidia spy scandal that led to Jensen Huang’s ouster as CEO poured more fuel on the fire, igniting additional worries that his “circular” financing deals would unravel and leave neocloud companies in its ecosystem without capital for new data centers or AI chips.

In addition, revelations that China had backdoor access to high-end U.S. chips used in AI development are spurring a federal crackdown to close loopholes in export restrictions. Trump even vowed to stop U.S. companies from building data centers abroad.

Moody’s Analytics Chief Economist Mark Zandi warned in a social media post that the stock market selloff could weigh on economic growth via the wealth effect, which affects consumer spending.

He estimated that that consumer spending rises or falls by about 2 cents for every $1 increase or decrease in net worth over about a year.

That means that if stock prices stay where they are, the wealth effect will subtract almost 0.3 percentage points from real GDP growth a year from now, after adding 0.7 percentage points in this quarter.

“We’ve seen AI stocks selloff before, only for them to rebound quickly. Investors have been conditioned to buy on the dip,” Zandi wrote. “But while there are sure to be lots of ups and downs in stock prices in the days ahead, it feels increasingly like the easy money in the AI trade has been made. If so, the economy won’t be able to count on AI to be the sole engine of growth.”

But the end of the year also tends to lighten the mood on Wall Street and lift stocks. While the traditional “Santa Claus rally” is still weeks away, the upcoming shortened week could provide some early relief.

Markets will be closed for Thanksgiving on Thursday and open for just a half day on Friday. Thin trading volumes could also amplify stock rebounds.

Meanwhile, Wall Street forecasters remain upbeat about 2027 even as markets are in corrections. Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs expect the S&P 500 to finish next year at 8,700. Meanwhile, UBS Global Wealth Management and Wells Fargo see 8,200.

Then there’s Steve Chiavarone, chief investment officer for equities at Federated Hermes, who has a year-end view of 10,000—or a 45% surge from current levels.

He brushed aside this month’s midterm elections, which saw Democrats sweep Congress and several state capitals. While Wall Street fears the blue tsunami will slow the AI infrastructure boom, Chiavarone said risks to the buildout are overblown. Even a slight retreat would be positive.

“A modest pullback in the data center buildout could give cash flows time to catch up, easing inflation pressures and making the investment boom more sustainable,” he argued.

item.title: Alibaba and Tencent put their faith in Chinese chips as U.S. curbs threatens to slow down their AI development
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: In-depth analysis of the impact of US chip restrictions on Chinese tech giants, with useful vocabulary

Tencent and Alibaba said this week that domestic chips can cushion their cloud businesses from new U.S. restrictions on access to advanced AI processors, yet acknowledged that they could still slow the development of new AI models.

Both tech giants reported earnings after the U.S. Department of Commerce released an interim rule expanding export controls on Monday, making them some of the first Chinese corporate responses to the restrictions.

Chipmakers and exporters now need a license to sell advanced chips to data centers in Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil. The rule also requires a license for large data centers to offer substantial computing power to Chinese customers. Together, the measures are likely to restrict the amount of computing power available to Chinese companies like Alibaba and Tencent as they develop AI models and offer them to users.

Tencent

Tencent executives, in the company’s earnings call, drew a distinction between the computing power needed to train new models and running existing ones.

“We actually don’t see an impact because our cloud business today is primarily running inference,” James Mitchell, Tencent’s chief strategy officer, told analysts on Wednesday. (Inference is the running of AI models, as opposed to training them.)

Mitchell added that Tencent had reached a stage where the inference could run on what he called a “surprisingly limited number” of domestically produced chips.

Martin Lau, Tencent’s president, agreed that the domestic supply chain should be able to cover inference, particularly for Tencent’s smaller, more efficient models.

Still, Lau called the restrictions “unfortunate” and admitted that it would now take longer for Tencent to train the next version of its Hunyuan model. “It sets everyone back in China,” he said.

In the long run, Lau predicted that U.S. controls would “speed up” the development of China’s domestic chip industry. “We believe all Chinese players would actually have to rely on domestic supply chains and domestic chips.”

Tencent reported 207.3 billion yuan ($31 billion) in revenue for the third quarter of 2026, up 8% year-on-year. Fintech and business services revenue, which includes cloud computing, rose 9.4% to reach 63.6 billion yuan ($9.5 billion).

Net profit rose 0.3% to 65.1 billion yuan ($9.8 billion). Capital expenditure rose 527% to 81.4 billion yuan ($12.2 billion).

Alibaba

On Thursday, on its earnings call, Alibaba said its 2030 targets—including $100 billion in external cloud revenue and a 20% EBITDA margin—remain on track despite the new restrictions.

“Our own progress in developing domestic computing power is in fact already ahead of our original expectations,” Alibaba CEO Eddie Wu told analysts on the call. The company has invested heavily in its in-house chip division, T-Head, which it plans to list in Hong Kong.

Alibaba reported 271.5 billion yuan ($40.5 billion) in revenue for the third quarter of 2026, up 10% year-on-year. AI and cloud revenue rose 53% to reach 61.0 billion yuan ($9.1 billion).

Net profit also rose by 213% year-on-year to 64.4 billion yuan ($9.6 billion). Capital expenditure rose by 60% to reach 50.5 billion yuan ($7.5 billion).

Alibaba’s confidence in its longer-term targets came with a warning about the near term.

“The new compute export control rules will affect next year’s products and services, and there is still uncertainty as regards the supply chain,” Wu said during the earnings call. He suggested that cloud revenue growth could slow to between 30% and 45%, then rebound to 50% or higher by 2028.

Wu said it was “too early at this stage” to know how U.S. restrictions might affect the development of its Qwen family of models, though he added that the company’s current T-Head chips “are already capable of fully supporting the training of large-scale, including ultra-large-scale, models.” Wu predicted that T-Head production would ramp up in 2027 or 2028. “Once we get there, we will actually be in a better position to control and pace the speed at which we iterate our foundation models,” he said.

Alibaba, however, is in the spotlight after the Nvidia scandal, which toppled CEO Jensen Huang last week. Nvidia’s sales team introduced Alibaba to Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive, before U.S. chip export controls took effect in 2022, the Information reported. Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud computing company, is suspected of funneling advanced AI chips to China in violation of U.S. export controls; Megaspeed denies the allegations.

On Thursday, a group of Alibaba shareholders sued the company, accusing it of concealing its ties to Alice Huang and Megaspeed. The shareholders said media reports of the ties contributed to a 14% drop in Alibaba’s share price over four days, and accused it of understating the risk that export-control violations could harm its business.

Alibaba did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Chip controls

The Commerce Department faces increased scrutiny over whether it has done enough to keep advanced chips out of China. On Thursday, the House Foreign Affairs Committee released data showing the department had approved nearly 880,000 AI chips for Chinese companies—including 75,000 for Alibaba and 150,000 for Tencent—out of more than 3.4 million chips that Nvidia and AMD sought to export to Chinese companies.

Chinese AI developers beyond Tencent and Alibaba are preparing for the likely impact of tighter U.S. chip restrictions. The Information reported Thursday that Moonshot AI, the Beijing-based developer of the Kimi models, had scrapped a $150 million deal to access Nvidia’s Blackwell chips through an Indonesian data center.…

Source: Fortune | Published: 2026-11-20 12:44 UTC | Difficulty: 70/100

item.title: Energy bills will soar - here's how you can ease the pain
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Practical advice on managing energy bills with clear, well-structured English

Energy bills will soar - here's how you can ease the pain

Energy prices are forecast to rise by 26% for millions of homes in January, but experts say there are ways to keep a check on rising bills.

Here are four areas to consider ahead of the increase.

1. Practical ways to reduce your energy use

Energy regulator Ofgem's price cap, as well as suppliers' fixed deals, set a limit on the price of each unit of energy, not the total bill.

So, you pay for what you use. Millions of people have cut back on their energy consumption during years of relatively high prices.

With the unit price of gas, in particular, set to soar, experts say you should take a fresh look at your energy use and renew good habits.

Research foundation Nesta suggests:

- turning down the flow temperature on a combi boiler - usually indicated by a radiator icon, to make it operate more efficiently

- turning off the pre-heat facility on some combi boilers, which would have kept some water heated up when not in use

- turning down the thermostat one degree, although 18C is the recommended minimum

- closing all curtains at night

- lowering radiator valves outside of the living room

- turning off the heating before April

These are small changes but - alongside washing clothes at 30C, blocking draughts and batch cooking - they can reduce energy use and bills.

2. Pay by direct debit

Ofgem says about five million people still pay their bill when it arrives every three months, rather than receive a monthly bill often initially based on an estimate.

Taking regular meter readings, or having a smart meter, while paying by monthly direct debit solves that problem.

Paying by direct debit costs significantly less than by so-called standard credit - typically Â£138 cheaper a year.

Customers on prepayment schemes - usually people on low incomes struggling to pay bills - used to pay a higher rate than others, but now they pay slightly less than the capped direct debit variable rate.

Various deals may rely on paying by direct debit or having a smart meter.

3. Consider switching to a fixed rate

Moving to a fixed energy tariff means the price you are charged per unit of gas or electricity does not change every three months, although the total bill will still vary depending on how much energy you use.

The trouble is that it is very difficult to work out whether a fixed deal is a good deal at the moment, for those renewing fixed deals or looking for one for the first time.

Some fixed deals are available at unit prices below the next forecast price cap level. But should energy prices fall sharply then a longer-term fix might not seem such good value compared with the price cap.

So consumer group Which? also recommends paying close attention to any exit fees when picking a fixed deal. If variable prices fall below your fixed rate and you want to get out of it before the end of your agreement period, you may have to pay a hefty sum.

Before you fix, consumer website MoneySavingExpert advises you look at all the deals available, not just what your own supplier is offering.

4. Check what financial support you can get

The government will give a Â£100 payment to millions of homes to help cover winter energy costs. It will go to homes in council tax bands A to D in England, with the equivalent expected in Scotland and Wales.

There are also a range of other forms of support specifically for people on low incomes.

This winter anyone on means-tested benefits will get Â£150 off their electricity bill.

Your supplier will apply the discount automatically unless you are in Scotland, where you will need to contact your energy company to ask for the help.

Some people will also be eligible for a Cold Weather Payment, external and most pensioners will receive the winter fuel payment.

Beyond that, most energy suppliers offer hardship grants for people struggling to pay their bills and the government's Fuel Direct Scheme, external can help you repay energy debt.

You can get more advice from Ofgem, external, Citizens Advice, external, or your own energy supplier. Trade body Energy UK has a list of support schemes, external.

People on low incomes may also be eligible for grants to help with insulating their homes, and there are local schemes offering grants for solar panels, heat pumps and the like.

But if you are hunting around for grants, watch out for scams pretending to be official money-off schemes.

Source: BBC Business | Published: 2026-11-23 01:05 UTC | Difficulty: 50/100

item.title: Intuit moves to sell Mailchimp for $3.68 billion as AI reshapes its growth strategy
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Detailed explanation of Intuit's strategic shift and the role of AI, with useful vocabulary

Good morning.

The QuickBooks and TurboTax parent announced Thursday it plans to sell Mailchimp, an email marketing automation platform, to Bending Spoons for approximately $3.68 billion. The deal is expected to close in early 2027, subject to approval, with proceeds earmarked for fiscal 2027 share repurchases. Intuit paid approximately $12 billion for Mailchimp in 2021. Mailchimp’s quarterly revenue fell 1% to $313 million.

Sasan Goodarzi, CEO of Intuit (No. 231 on the Fortune 500) said on the earnings call that Intuit still wants to help businesses manage lead-to-cash needs, but believes it can do so more effectively by building AI-powered capabilities into QuickBooks rather than owning Mailchimp.

Mailchimp sale marks strategic shift

The divestiture adds another dimension to what CFO Sandeep Aujla has called Intuit’s “reset to reaccelerate” strategy launched in August: accepting some near-term pressure on revenue per customer to rebuild customer acquisition. The strategy includes lower upfront revenue per TurboTax customer as Intuit seeks faster customer growth.

The latest results offered evidence of operating momentum. For the fiscal first quarter ended Oct. 31, revenue rose 12% to $4.35 billion, while adjusted earnings per share increased 56% to $2.91. Both exceeded analyst expectations.

In my conversation with Aujla, he pointed to mid-market revenue growth of 41% and customer growth of 30% as evidence that Intuit’s major growth initiatives are gaining traction. He also emphasized management’s commitment to delivering on its promises.

But the outlook exposed pressure at Credit Karma from tighter financing conditions and changing consumer behavior.

Intuit now forecasts fiscal 2027 revenue of $23.08 billion to $23.37 billion, lowering its outlook to reflect slower expected growth at Credit Karma amid tighter lending conditions and changing consumer behavior. It maintained its adjusted earnings forecast of $22.88 to $23.12 a share. Neither forecast includes the pending Mailchimp sale. The stock was down about 13% in after-hours trading.

Aujla said conditions have shifted since Intuit set its guidance in August, when the debate centered on whether the Federal Reserve would hold interest rates steady or lower them. He described the environment now as one of tightening, with higher rates slowing consumer demand in the categories Credit Karma serves. Lending partners are still expanding, he said, but at a slower pace.

AI reshapes Credit Karma’s customer acquisition

At the same time, changes in how consumers seek financial information are affecting Credit Karma.

“The evolution of consumer behavior is impacting us faster than what we had anticipated,” Aujla told me.

Historically, only about 1% of Credit Karma’s customers came through search engines, he said. Now, consumers increasingly turn to AI for initial answers before visiting Credit Karma, creating a new customer acquisition challenge.

“More customers are going to AI to get the first answer,” he said.

Intuit plans to apply lessons from QuickBooks and TurboTax to improve Credit Karma’s visibility in AI-generated responses, Aujla said. AI is thus both a product opportunity and a customer acquisition challenge.

Regarding the market’s reaction, Aujla said that during major technological shifts, whether cloud computing, mobile or now AI, “it’s just human nature to overreact to the uncertainty and the pendulum swings.” He sees the reaction as an overcorrection, with investors questioning whether companies can successfully navigate the changes.

“What we are underwriting is, in our 40-plus years of history, we’ve been able to evolve and continue to come out of every change in the marketplace,” he said.

Have a good weekend.

Sheryl Estrada

Sheryl.Estrada@fortune.com

Leaderboard

Fortune 500 Power Moves

Erik Uitenbogaart was named vice president of finance and CFO at Citgo Petroleum Corporation, (No. 24) effective Nov. 16. Uitenbogaart joins Citgo from LyondellBasell, where he held roles of increasing responsibility since 2013, most recently as vice president of finance, strategy and M&A for Sustainable Solutions. He previously led LyondellBasell’s global financial planning and analysis organization. Before that, he served as controller for Europe, the Middle East and Africa at Univar Solutions and spent more than 15 years at PricewaterhouseCoopers.

Richard McPhail, EVP and CFO of The Home Depot (No. 25), was promoted to CEO, effective Nov. 23. McPhail will succeed Ted Decker, who has returned from a temporary medical leave of absence, but will step down as president and CEO, and he will continue to serve as chair of the board of directors. McPhail joined the company in 2005 and was named EVP and CFO in September 2019.

Jordan Broggi was promoted to EVP and CFO at The Home Depot. Broggi is a 13-year veteran of the company, most recently serving as EVP of interconnected retail. In this role, he led the online business and customer experience for the company's digital properties, as well as loyalty, credit services and payments. Broggi has held several leadership positions during his tenure, including senior vice president of finance.

Zach Davis was promoted to president and CFO at Cheniere Energy, Inc. (No. 223). Davis was previously executive vice president and CFO. Davis has served as CFO of Cheniere since August 2020 and also serves as a director and CFO of the general partner of Cheniere Energy Partners, L.P. He joined Cheniere in 2013 and previously served as SVP of finance and VP of finance and planning. Davis has over 20 years of experience, primarily in energy and infrastructure finance.

The weekly Fortune 500 Power Moves column tracks Fortune 500 company C-suite shifts—see the most recent edition.

item.title: I moved from Australia to the Welsh valleys because the houses are so cheap
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Engaging story with clear details on housing affordability, suitable for English learners

I moved from Australia to the Welsh valleys because the houses are so cheap

A house-hunter has moved 10,000 miles (16,000km) from Australia to Wales' most affordable town because the properties are so cheap.

James Brown, 56, spotted the three-bed house in Tylorstown, near Ferndale, Rhondda Cynon Taf, online for Â£80,000 and put an offer in.

Originally from the Midlands, Brown said the equivalent property in his home region would have cost him Â£200,000.

"It's ideal if you're commuting, and everything's virtually on your doorstep, so a really affordable area to come to," he said.

But some people who live in Ferndale - dubbed Wales' most affordable town with an average property price of Â£116,200 - say they are still struggling to buy homes.

Zoopla says a typical home in Ferndale costs "less than twice the annual wages of two full-time workers".

The property selling website said its analysis shows this is the most affordable town in Wales.

Residents have described how they have had to travel to work in England to afford a home in the area, while an estate agent said the low prices attract investors and buy-to-rent landlords from outside south Wales.

Brown said: "It's definitely a lot of outside buyers buying properties in Wales which I suppose in some ways is not helping the local people get on the ladder, but like I said, the affordability is just unreal in south Wales."

Emma Weston, 36, who runs a cafÃ© in Ferndale said she had to make the choice between using savings to invest in her business or buying a house.

"Obviously, I chose to keep my job and put the money here," she said.

My partner, he's an electrician, a good trade, I obviously manage a business.

"We still have money but there's nothing left in the pot whereby I can say we can save X-amount to put down to a deposit."

Weston knows property is more expensive elsewhere, but says Ferndale still does not feel affordable.

"I've lived outside of the valleys, therefore I can see the comparisons," she said.

"However, if you look at the cost of living crisis, which we're all facing, everything is just costing an absolute bomb."

CafÃ© customer Marcus, 31, took a job nearly 100 miles (165km) away in Somerset so he could afford a family home.

"Moving to my new job gave that opportunity to buy the house," he said.

Weston said he liked the security of having his own home, and sees it as an investment for his children.

But he said: "I think if you were living in London, Reading... Birmingham... I'd say it is the easiest place to get a property because the house value here and there is completely different.

"For us, it's hard. For people coming into Wales is easy and is affordable."

Estate agent David Ricketts said the south Wales valleys are attractive to people outside the area.

"You're getting more for your money, there's less stress, there's a lower mortgage to pay and it's an area which I think will get better and better, it'll grow and you'd get a lovely welcome in any valleys town," he said.

Ricketts said some buyers were not necessarily looking to live there themselves.

"What you've got now is a situation, not only just to buy, you have investors coming in because they've realised that the rental yield is quite reasonable and that will only grow," he said.

"These are very attractive areas to live and also to be a landlord."

Donna Thomas, 41, rents in Maerdy with her partner and their three children.

They rent because a mortgage is too expensive.

"If we're happy where we are, why change that? Why go into an even more stressful situation rather than just stay where we are and make do with what we have?

"It would be more stress, and everything would be harder, the money wouldn't stretch as far and the thing is we want to give the girls the best life that we possibly can with what we have," she said.

Thomas said she was happy for investors to buy properties in the area and rent them back to locals.

She said: "It means that when you can't afford to get a mortgage on a house that you really like, if somebody else did buy it, and then rented it out to you, I would say that would be really good.

"I think I can't afford to get a mortgage on this house, but I really like this house, and now I'm renting it."

Chiropractor Ellie Thomas, 25, lives with her parents in Ferndale.

She is saving up for a deposit on a house near a city.

"I don't think I would want to live here," she said.

"I just feel like there's not much going on here. Most of the shops are shut. There's like one cafÃ©, a few hairdressers, there's not really much."

However, she understands it was likely to be more expensive and harder to buy elsewhere.

"Obviously, it's a bit hard to find somewhere nice in the area you want for an affordable price," she said.

"It would be easier for me to live here.

"It's a lovely community, everyone knows each other, but it's just a bit far out of the way, and petrol is expensive now too."

Source: BBC Business | Published: 2026-11-23 06:03 UTC | Difficulty: 50/100

item.title: Pip assessments need 'fundamental overhaul', report to say
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Discussion of the Pip assessment process with useful vocabulary and context

Pip assessments need 'fundamental overhaul', report to say

A review into the personal independence payment (Pip) will call for a "fundamental overhaul" of the assessment process to "better recognise people's varying costs and needs", the disability minister has said.

Sir Stephen Timms has been looking into disability benefits for the past year and found the set up was "no longer fit for purpose".

Writing in the Times, external, he said his review, to be published in full on Tuesday, would recommend people with the most severe conditions have a "fast track" process which is "less burdensome".

It comes after a separate review into young people not in education, employment or training (Neets) recommended Pip be scrapped and replaced for under-25s.

Sir Stephen said that while Pip had the "right aims" when it was created, there have been "marked shifts in the nature of disability and ill health" in the 13 years since.

He said there had been "substantial growth in claims for mental health and neurodiverse conditions as well as changes to wider society and the workplace".

"For those with the most severe conditions and end of life care, the review recommends a fast track which is less burdensome, with assessment capacity freed up for other cases," he said.

"Someone with a lifelong or degenerative illness should not need regular reassessments which feel adversarial and unnecessary."

He added: "Disabled people must have the chance to participate fully in everyday life, including in work, and need a more personalised, flexible system that supports them to do so, rather than itself being a barrier."

The Timms review was commissioned after a U-turn from former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer's government on a plan for major benefit reform in an attempt to reduce the welfare bill by Â£5bn a year.

More than 130 MPs, including 120 from Labour, signed an amendment to reject plans to cut disability and sickness-related benefit payments in 2025.

The rebels said they opposed the plans because of the number of people expected to be pushed into relative poverty and a lack of consultation at the time.

The government accepted recommendations from the Milburn review to move those aged 18 to 24 off Pip and the health element of universal credit, and onto an entirely new benefits system.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he thought the "same philosophy" could be applied "right through the age range".

At this stage it is unclear how both of the reviews will complement one another.

The cost of Pip is expected to rise to more than Â£41bn by 2030, up from Â£15bn in 2020. It was being claimed by 4m people in the UK as of 30 April 2026, according to the Department for Work and Pensions.

Though reforming the benefit has frequently been looked at as a way to reduce the Treasury's welfare bill, disability charities have described it as a lifeline for many.

Ahead of the Timms review being handed down, disability equality charity Scope said ministers must ensure Pip is not weakened.

"Life costs more when you're disabled, whether you work or not," executive director James Taylor said, adding that Pip was "vital financial support".

"We know there is real fear among disabled people that changes could leave them unable to afford the essentials."

item.title: What is going on with Poundland?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Analysis of Poundland's situation with clear details, though not as in-depth as other articles

What is going on with Poundland?

The future of Poundland hangs in the balance as it faces a possible collapse into administration.

Its owner, US investment firm Gordon Brothers, put it up for sale in September, but then rejected offers to keep the business afloat.

Poundland has a major presence on the High Street, with 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, where it trades under the Dealz brand.

If it were to collapse, the jobs of its 11,000 employees would be at risk, as well as potentially thousands of others at firms that supply the retailer.

How have we got here?

Have people stopped shopping at Poundland?

People have not stopped shopping at Poundland - quite the opposite.

Although the chain was struggling when it was sold by Pepco last year for Â£1, the business turned a corner over the year to September, going from a Â£68m loss to an Â£18.1m profit before interest, tax and certain accounting charges.

Going into the vital Christmas period, first-quarter like-for-like sales were up 7% and operational profits of Â£1.9m were up Â£1.2m on last year.

Halloween sales were 11.4% higher than last year - this is usually a good indicator of how a retailer will do at Christmas, says retail analyst Catherine Shuttleworth of Savvy Marketing.

According to Julie Palmer, managing partner at insolvency specialist Begbies Traynor: "This isn't a story about shoppers abandoning Poundland. The tills are busier than they were a year ago."

She adds: "On the face of it, a turnaround seems well under way."

However, Gordon Brothers has been restricting Poundland's access to cash needed to restock stores and meet day-to-day expenses.

It had frozen about Â£50m in funds leading to concerns Poundland's shops would run out of stock.

However, Gordon Brothers released around Â£21m over two weeks recently, giving the chain a little more breathing space.

So why is it facing administration?

Poundland seems to be facing "a funding and ownership problem rather than a trading collapse", Palmer says.

However, while Poundland boss Barry Williams says the business is making a "strong recovery", Gordon Brothers has painted a different picture, saying the chain remains "challenged and vulnerable to any potential downturn in future trading".

It says it has provided significant funding to support the company's ability to trade since it acquired the business.

It has also made about Â£18m from a combination of debt interest payments and other fees and charges.

As well as being Poundland's owner, it is one of its lenders, and is owed loans, including a Â£22.5m shareholder loan it inherited when it bought the business for Â£1.

As the main creditor, Gordon Brothers would be first in line to get paid back if the business goes under - but its suppliers are not.

"When the owner is also the main lender, its first priority is recovering [loans]," says Palmer. "Sometimes the route that best protects the lender is different from the one that saves the most jobs, and that tension is why this has become such a political story."

Irish firm Martin Property Group has offered to buy the business as a going concern, while London-based holding company Xyra Group has also made a rescue bid, although doubts remain about the credibility of Xyra's offer.

There is also a third, unnamed bid on the table.

Gordon Brothers has also been weighing options to break Poundland up.

The US company's view is that ultimately breaking the retailer up will provide more security for employees in the long term, because any buyers of its store estate will also have to agree to keep the employees on.

Insiders who are critical of how Gordon Brothers has handled the Poundland sale say it is driving the business into the ground to make money through the insolvency process.

But the investment firm, which specialises in buying and restructuring distressed companies, has denied the claim.

What future does Poundland have?

For now, Poundland has avoided immediate collapse after a deadline was extended by 10 days to find a rescue deal.

Shuttleworth says the future of Poundland is "really unclear, with the owners and the management at loggerheads about its future".

Palmer says there are two ways forward for Poundland - either a solvent deal, where the company gets bought and carries on trading, or a collapse followed by a break-up.

"The immediate make-or-break issue is Christmas: a value retailer that can't get stock on its shelves in November and December is in serious trouble, whatever its full-year results say," says Palmer.

There has been political pressure on Gordon Brothers from both Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds. They have called for answers over why the Martin Property Group offer to buy the business, which would have protected jobs, was rejected.

A committee of MPs also questioned Gordon Brothers last week, adding to pressure.

But Shuttleworth says that as a US firm Gordon Brothers appears "unmoved" by the arguments that the UK government has put forward.

item.title: Can government be the catalyst for breakthrough innovation?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Exploration of government's role in innovation with moderate complexity

We help you solve the problems that matter most so you can act faster and move further.

Take on Tomorrow

Can government be the catalyst for breakthrough innovation?

S04E07

Big breakthrough innovations are on the horizon, and they could be coming from an unlikely place. We’re talking about the sort of ideas that would reshape how we move, the medical treatments we receive, and how we adapt to the changing climate and generate new kinds of energy—and they could all stem from a space not typically associated with innovation: the government. Rethinking the public sector’s role in innovation—and how it works together with private industry—may be key to solving the world’s most pressing challenges and improving people’s lives.

Listen and subscribe

In this episode of Take on Tomorrow, hosts Lizzie O’Leary and Femi Oke talk to Rafael Laguna de la Vera, Director of Germany’s Federal Agency for Breakthrough Innovation (SPRIND), about why governments should be funding innovation across industries. Plus: Frederik Blachetta, Public Sector Data & AI Leader from PwC Germany, talks to us about how business can work alongside government to drive positive change.

RAFAEL LAGUNA DE LA VERA: Government can change law. Government can put a lot of money at stuff, even more than any rich individual could do. Government is actually required to scale businesses.

FREDERIK BLACHETTA: There’s always those kind of theories, where we are arguing that governments are the problem. I would really love to see governments change that view and really be innovative drivers.

RAFAEL LAGUNA DE LA VERA: The big questions of our day are global. And it doesn’t really matter all that much who solves them as long as they get solved. The first breakthrough innovation of us is us. You know, we’ve invented a government agency that acts very differently from others.

LIZZIE O’LEARY: Across the world, it’s not just the private sector seeing an opportunity for innovative growth. Governments are also stepping into the fold. Helping to accelerate big ideas across industries, fostering new kinds of partnerships—and improving lives.

FEMI OKE: So could the world’s next big breakthrough innovation be driven by government?

LIZZIE: And what does that mean for the way the public and private sector work together?

FEMI: I’m Femi Oke, a broadcaster and journalist.

LIZZIE: And I’m Lizzie O’Leary, a podcaster and journalist. And this is a special series of Take on Tomorrow, the podcast from PwC’s management publication, strategy and business.

FEMI: Today, we ask: what’s the role of government in driving innovation, as we look at how we Govern and Serve?

LIZZIE: To help us understand how the relationship between business and government works today—and could work in the future—we’re delighted to be joined by Frederik Blachetta, Public Sector Data & AI Leader from PwC Germany. Frederik, welcome to the show!

FREDERIK: Nice to be here.

FEMI: So, we talk a lot on this podcast about the role of businesses in driving innovation, but why should we be paying attention to what governments do in this space?

FREDERIK: Well, I think there’ several reasons for that. I think the first and foremost is, if we look into the history, all kinds of groundbreaking innovations that have come to us in the past: be it the smartphone with the haptic touch on the front, or some other inventions, [they] wouldn’t have been possible without funding. And also the risk-taking of governments in that state. I mean, we have tremendous examples of that. I think some things, especially if they’re [at] an early stage, are really complicated to figure out risk-wise. I think to close this kind of gap is also something where governments could really help us through.

LIZZIE: Frederik, before you came to PwC, you actually worked in government at the German Federal Chancellery. So you’ve experienced government from within. How has government worked alongside businesses traditionally, and do you think we’re seeing a shift in how those relationships come together right now?

FREDERIK: Well, I think first and foremost, it’s very important to reiterate, everyone is always trying to say, like, governments are very slow, and it’s on governments that things are not happening at this point of time. I think you can also easily say that about some big corporations, which are sometimes also full of politics, and full of that kind of stuff. So, governments are not that slow, as some might think. And furthermore, I think governments, especially the people that work at governments, really have a kind of mission. So they really want to change something for the best of societies. I think if you look into what governments are doing and how they’re working with privates, I think we really see a trend in changing of doing everything on their own to changing to a more capability-driven ecosystem approach in which the, kind of, borders are thinner, sometimes even making it possible to change back and forth just as I did—or others. But, of course, also, to really work together and work in a very cooperative way. We have to see, like, what can we take from privates? What can we easily adapt upon? Where can we use the capabilities that they are having to really make government work better? And this is what governments are doing at this moment. And I think this is not possible without private sector.

LIZZIE: Frederik, thank you so much. We’re going to come back to you in just a bit to hear more about the role government plays alongside business later. But first, Femi, you’ve been hearing all about how the German government is focusing on innovation.…
